why_this_tool: Temporal is the tool the lesson is built around, and its local development server lets you practise durable execution, replay, activity retries and message passing end to end on a laptop.
alternatives: Apache Airflow and Dagster schedule batch DAGs rather than long-lived event-driven processes; AWS Step Functions is a managed state machine defined in JSON rather than code; Argo Workflows runs container steps on Kubernetes without replay-based durability; Kafka or RabbitMQ with hand-written consumers gives messaging but leaves state, retries and timers to you.

setup.do: Install Python 3.9 or newer, create a virtual environment and install the Temporal Python SDK by following the Python quickstart.
setup.done_when: Importing the temporalio package in the virtual environment succeeds without an error.
setup.why: The whole path is written against one SDK, and the Python SDK is the one most ML platform code already sits next to.

setup.do: Install the Temporal CLI and start the local development server, then open its Web UI in a browser.
setup.done_when: The Web UI loads and shows the default namespace with an empty list of Workflow Executions.
setup.why: The development server is a single binary holding the whole Temporal Service, so no cloud account or cluster is needed to practise.

setup.do: Create a project folder with four separate files: workflow definitions, activity definitions, a worker program and a client starter script.
setup.done_when: The folder holds the four files and each can be imported without an error.
setup.why: A Temporal Application is split into these parts, and keeping them apart from the start makes the determinism boundary between workflows and activities visible.

steps.do: Run the quickstart hello-world workflow end to end: start the worker, start the workflow from the client script and read the result.
steps.done_when: The client prints the workflow result and the Web UI lists one Workflow Execution with status Completed.
steps.why: A first run proves the server, the worker and the client can talk to each other before you write anything of your own.

steps.do: Write a model promotion workflow that calls three activities in order: validate the model, run an evaluation, then publish it to a registry stub.
steps.done_when: Starting the promotion workflow completes and the Web UI shows the three activities scheduled and completed in order.
steps.why: A workflow is ordinary code describing the steps of a long-running process, and a promotion pipeline is the kind of ML platform process Temporal fits best.

steps.do: Start two worker processes that poll the same named task queue, then start several promotion workflows and note which worker identity picks up each task.
steps.done_when: The Web UI shows both worker identities polling the task queue and tasks handled by each of them.

source.title: What is a Temporal Worker? | Temporal Documentation

steps.why: Workers are your own processes that run workflow and activity code, and scaling means adding processes on the same task queue rather than changing the server.

steps.do: Start a promotion workflow while no worker is running, watch it stay in Running, then start a worker and watch it proceed.
steps.done_when: The execution stays Running with a scheduled workflow task and no progress until the worker starts, then completes.
steps.why: The Matching Service holds tasks in task queues until a worker polls, which is why the server never calls your code and workers can sit inside a private ML network.

steps.do: Query the full Event History of one finished promotion workflow in the Web UI and with the CLI, and match each event to a line of your workflow code.
steps.done_when: You can point at the events for the workflow start, each activity being scheduled, started and completed, and the workflow completion.

source.title: Events and Event History | Temporal Documentation

steps.why: The Event History is the durable record of everything the workflow did, and reading it is the main debugging skill for Temporal.

steps.do: Run a promotion workflow with a slow evaluation activity, kill the worker process in the middle, then restart it and watch the workflow resume.
steps.done_when: The workflow completes after the restart and the validate activity appears only once in the Event History.
steps.why: Durable execution means the restarted worker rebuilds workflow state by replaying the history instead of re-running completed steps.

steps.do: Configure a start-to-close timeout, a retry policy and a heartbeat timeout on the evaluation activity, make it fail twice and then stall, and pass an idempotency key to the publish activity.
steps.done_when: The history shows the activity attempt count rising, a heartbeat timeout failure recorded, and the registry stub holds one published entry despite retries.

source.title: Events and Event History | Temporal Documentation

steps.why: Side effects live in activities, which the platform retries and times out according to policy, so each activity must be safe to run more than once.

steps.do: Write a signal that delivers a human approval, a query that returns the current promotion stage and an update that changes the target environment and returns the validated value.
steps.done_when: The workflow waits until the approval signal arrives, the query returns the stage without adding events to the history, and the update returns its result to the caller.

source.title: Temporal Workflow message passing - Signals, Queries, & Updates | Temporal Documentation

verified.section_found: How to choose between Signals, Updates, and Queries as a Workflow author?

steps.why: Signals, queries and updates turn a workflow into an event-driven service, and each suits a different kind of request: write, read, or read and write.

steps.do: Start the development server with a database file so state persists, restart the server while a workflow waits for approval, then compare the histories of an approved run and a rejected run.
steps.done_when: After the server restart the waiting workflow is still listed as Running, and you can name the first event at which the two runs differ.
steps.why: The persistence layer is what makes histories survive a server restart, and comparing two histories side by side shows exactly where runs diverged.

steps.do: Create a non-deterministic change by adding a new activity before the evaluation step while a workflow is waiting for approval, observe the failure, then fix it with a patch.
steps.done_when: The unpatched change produces a non-determinism error on the workflow task, and with the patch the old execution completes while new executions run the new activity.
steps.why: Replay requires workflow code to issue the same commands as the history recorded, so changes to running workflow code must be versioned.

steps.do: Reproduce past executions by downloading their Event Histories as JSON and writing a replay test that runs them against the current workflow code in a pinned environment such as a CI job.
steps.done_when: The replay test passes on the patched code and fails when the patch is removed.

source.title: Events and Event History | Temporal Documentation

steps.why: Replaying saved histories in automation catches non-deterministic changes before a deploy rather than in running workflows.

steps.do: Deploy a self-hosted Temporal Service locally with containers and PostgreSQL as the database, point your workers and client at it, and run the promotion workflow there; Temporal Cloud is paid, so this local stack is the substitute.
steps.done_when: The promotion workflow completes against the containerised service and its history is still there after the containers are restarted.

source.title: Temporal Platform production deployments | Temporal Documentation

steps.why: Production runs the server as separate services with a real database and workers deployed apart from it, which the single-binary development server hides.
